The Reformers largely rejected monastic vows as unbiblical, and Protestant churches generally have no monastic orders. Some Anglican and Lutheran communities and newer 'new monastic' movements keep forms of communal life.

senses.definition: Having or employing multiple modes.
senses.example: multimodal transport

core.definition: In AI, able to process or produce more than one kind of data, such as text, images and audio.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress is on the first syllable, MUL. The ending '-al' is a weak syllable that sounds like 'ul', not 'all'. Keep the 'oh' clear in the middle syllable.

nuance.connotation: Neutral in technical use and positive in product marketing, where it suggests versatility.
nuance.usage_note: In the US, multimodal appears constantly in AI news, product launches and engineering talk, as in 'a multimodal model that reads images and text.' In a general sense it can mean using several senses or channels. The opposite in AI is unimodal, which means handling only one data type.

distinctions.note: Multisensory refers to several human senses; multimodal is broader and includes machine inputs and data types.
Multilingual means several languages, not several kinds of data.

examples.everyday: My phone's assistant is multimodal, so I can show it a photo and ask questions by voice.
examples.professional: We're evaluating a multimodal model that takes both support-ticket text and screenshots as input.
examples.analytical: A multimodal model must align representations across modalities so that text and image embeddings share a common space.

nuance.analogy: Like a translator who reads a book, looks at its pictures and listens to the author's voice, then summarizes all three together.
nuance.etymology: Multi- from Latin multus (many) plus modal, from Latin modus (measure, manner).
common_mistakes: Stressing the second syllable instead of MUL.
Confusing it with multilingual when talking about languages.

conversation.text: A multimodal model can take in more than one type of data, such as text, images, and audio.
Multimodal input lets the assistant read the chart in a screenshot, not just the surrounding text.
We evaluate multimodal reasoning on questions that require both the image and the text.

senses.definition: Resembling or characteristic of musk, especially in scent.
Muskellunge.

core.definition: Having a strong, sweet, heavy smell like musk, often used for perfume or a warm, animal-like scent.

pronunciation.tip: Stress is on the first syllable, and the vowel is short, like 'cut'. Do not stretch the vowel to 'moo'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive for perfume, and negative for a strong or stuffy smell.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use musky to describe perfume, cologne, or candles with a warm, heavy scent. For fish, Americans usually say muskie for the muskellunge, a large freshwater fish popular with anglers. Calling a room musky is less common and sounds more descriptive than casual.

distinctions.note: Musty means stale and damp, like an old basement. Musky means a warm, strong, sweet scent.
Floral describes flower-like scents. Musky describes heavier, warmer, animal-like notes.

examples.everyday: I like her perfume, but it is a little too musky for me in summer.
examples.professional: The scent team wants a musky base note for the candle, so let's test two options.
examples.analytical: The poet describes the room as musky, using smell to evoke intimacy and decay.

nuance.analogy: Like a warm, soft blanket that holds a scent long after you have taken it off.
nuance.etymology: From musk, from Persian and Sanskrit words for the scent gland of the musk deer, with the suffix -y.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the first vowel as 'oo'.
Using musky for the fish without knowing that Americans call it muskie in speech.

senses.definition: Having a value that is changeable during program execution.
Changeable, dynamic, evolutive; inclined to change, evolve, mutate.
Being one of the signs Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius and Pisces, associated with adaptability, flexibility and sympathy.
Something mutable; a variable or value that can change.

core.definition: Able to be changed; in programming, describing a value or object whose contents can be modified after it is created.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The final -able reduces to a light buhl, not a full vowel, and the t is a flap in General American.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a precise, descriptive term.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech, people say changeable or flexible. Mutable appears in writing, philosophy and especially programming, where a mutable object can be altered and an immutable one cannot. Do not confuse it with mutual, which means shared.

distinctions.note: Changeable is common and everyday; mutable is more formal and used for abstract or technical things.
A variable is a named container in programming; mutable describes whether the value it holds can change.

examples.everyday: My schedule is pretty mutable, so text me and we can work something out.
examples.professional: Lists in Python are mutable, so changing one list affects every reference to it, while tuples are immutable.
examples.analytical: If human nature is mutable, moral education can reshape character rather than merely reveal it.

nuance.analogy: A mutable object is like a whiteboard you can erase and rewrite; an immutable one is like ink carved into stone.
nuance.etymology: From Latin mutabilis, changeable, from mutare, to change.
common_mistakes: Confusing mutable with mutual
Stressing the second syllable instead of the first

mutable.etymology: From Middle English *mutable*, from Old French *mutable*, from Latin *mutabilis* (“liable to change”).

senses.definition: The person who will be served next.

core.definition: The person who will be served or will take a turn after everyone ahead of them in a queue.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on LINE. In fast speech 'next in' links into 'nex-tin,' and the final t of 'next' is often dropped before a consonant.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to positive; it signals fairness and waiting your turn.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use next in line at counters, deli counters, and checkout lines. Cashiers and clerks often say 'Next!' or 'You're next.' A natural reply is a short thanks or a nod. The phrase can also mean the next person eligible for a job or position.

distinctions.note: Next in order refers to sequence in a list; next in line refers to people or positions waiting for a turn.
First in line is the person at the front of the queue; next in line is the one after that.

examples.everyday: Excuse me, I think I'm next in line, so could you help me at the counter?
examples.professional: Once the current release is approved, the next in line is the infrastructure update, so please plan your sprint accordingly.
examples.analytical: In succession theory, the person next in line is defined by formal rules, which often matter more than personal qualifications.

nuance.analogy: Like a relay race where the next runner is already standing ready to take the baton.
nuance.etymology: 'Next' from Old English 'niehsta' (nearest), with 'line' from Latin 'linea.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'next on line' or 'next in the line' in standard American speech.
Using 'next in line' for a person already being served instead of the one after them.

conversation.text: I can help whoever's next in line.
Excuse me, are you next in line?
I was next in line when the register shut down.

senses.definition: Asking people not to reveal what happens in a show or movie.

core.definition: A warning shouted or typed to ask others not to reveal the plot or ending of a show or movie.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on SPOY in spoilers, and the -ers ending is a reduced rhotic syllable that sounds like 'erz'. The oy is a diphthong, so do not say it as 'oh'.

nuance.connotation: Playful and friendly; it protects other people's enjoyment and sounds fun.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say it before a show or movie is discussed, on social media, in group chats, or at family gatherings. It is casual and often used as an exclamation. A natural reply is 'Sorry, I'll keep it to myself' or 'Got it, no spoilers.'

distinctions.note: Spoiler alert warns that a spoiler is coming; no spoilers asks people not to reveal details at all.
Both are common; 'No spoilers!' is a direct request, while 'spoiler alert' is a warning before a statement.

examples.everyday: We're watching the finale tonight, so no spoilers, please!
examples.professional: I'm still catching up on the season, so no spoilers in the team channel, okay?
examples.analytical: Asking for no spoilers shows that narrative suspense is a shared value, since the meaning of a story can depend on its order of reveal.

nuance.analogy: Like covering your ears at a movie theater before the ending comes up.
common_mistakes: Writing 'no spoiler' in the singular when speaking to a group, although the plural is standard.
Saying 'spoil' with the wrong vowel; the word is stressed on the first syllable and ends in a clear z sound.

conversation.text: I haven't seen the finale yet, so no spoilers!
No spoilers! I'm watching it tonight.
No spoilers! I'm only on episode three.

senses.definition: Darkness; the absence of light.
The state of being unknown; a thing that is unknown.
senses.example: She was plucked from obscurity to star in a Broadway musical.

senses.definition: The quality of being difficult to understand; a thing that is difficult to understand.

core.definition: The state of being unknown, unimportant, or hard to see or understand; a thing that is not well known.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, SKYOO, and the final syllable is a light, reduced 'ee'. Do not stress the first syllable, and do not pronounce the r as a trill; the r is American rhotic and the 'ur' sound is a flap-like glide before the vowel.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative, suggesting something hidden, forgotten, or not recognized; it can describe a humble life positively, but usually implies lack of fame or clarity.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use obscurity most often for a person or work that has faded from attention, as in 'a band that rose from obscurity' or 'years of obscurity.' In everyday speech people would more often say 'nobody knows about it' or 'hardly anyone has heard of it,' so obscurity sounds slightly bookish in casual conversation. It is common in writing, journalism, and academic prose.

distinctions.note: Anonymity means the person's name is unknown or concealed, whereas obscurity means the person or thing is generally not famous or well known.
Ambiguity is a quality of language or meaning that can be read more than one way, while obscurity is a lack of clarity or fame in general.

examples.everyday: That little taco place was in obscurity for years until a food blogger wrote about it.
examples.professional: The old dashboard feature fell into obscurity after the redesign, so almost nobody on the team still uses it.
examples.analytical: The author's argument has largely fallen into obscurity, though its central claim about moral agency anticipates later debates.

nuance.analogy: Like a small town on a map that only the locals ever notice, a thing in obscurity is there but out of view.
nuance.etymology: From Latin obscurus, 'dark, covered over,' from obscurare, 'to darken.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the first syllable (OB-scurity) instead of the second.
Using obscurity for a single hard-to-understand passage; for that, say obscurity or 'an obscure passage' carefully, but usually 'ambiguity' or 'difficulty' is clearer.

obscurity.etymology: From Middle English *obscurite*, *obscuryte*, from Middle French *obscurité* and its etymon Latin *obscūritās*.

senses.definition: The part of the year when business is most slack and there are fewest clients or visitors.
senses.example: Seaside resorts in the off-season are really depressing.

senses.definition: A period of time when regular competitions are not being held, or when an athlete is not participating in competitions.
During the off-season.

core.definition: The period between sports seasons when games are not played, or the slow time of year for a business or resort.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the first syllable, and the second syllable 'season' carries secondary stress and reduces to 'zun'. Do not put strong stress on the second part, as in off-see-ZON.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Americans use offseason heavily in sports talk, as in 'in the offseason' for trades, training and free agency. In business, people also say 'slow season' or 'low season', and the adverb use is rare, so 'in the offseason' is the natural form. The hyphenated form off-season is also common in print.

distinctions.note: Preseason is the period just before the regular season begins, often with training camp and exhibition games, while offseason covers the longer break.
Postseason refers to playoffs or championship games after the regular season, while offseason is the time after the entire season finishes.
Slow season is a general business term for any quiet time, while offseason is mainly used for sports and seasonal activities.

examples.everyday: My dad says he has nothing to watch in the offseason, so he mostly reads the sports news.
examples.professional: Hotels in this resort town slow down in the offseason, so we cut staff from November to March.
examples.analytical: Teams use the offseason to reshape their rosters, and that quiet period often matters more to the franchise than the games themselves.

nuance.analogy: The offseason is like winter on a farm: no harvest is coming in, but the soil is being prepared for the next one.
nuance.etymology: From off, meaning away from the main time, plus season, ultimately from Latin satio, 'sowing'.
common_mistakes: Saying 'in offseason' without the article; Americans say 'in the offseason'.
Putting the main stress on the second syllable, as in off-SEA-son.

conversation.text: They made a lot of trades during the offseason.
What do football players do in the offseason?
The offseason is so boring when you're a big fan.

senses.definition: A person's daughter or son; a person's child.
senses.example: We are the offspring of Italian immigrants.

senses.definition: Any of a person's descendants, including of further generations.
An animal or plant's progeny or young.
Anything produced; the result of an entity's efforts.
senses.example: Artists often treasure their works as their immortal offspring.

senses.definition: A process launched by another process.

core.definition: A person's child or children, or the descendants of a person, animal, or plant.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, and the r in the middle is clearly pronounced in American English. Keep the vowel short, as in 'off', and don't add an extra syllable between the f and the sp.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It sounds more formal or technical than 'kids' or 'children', so it often appears in writing, legal or scientific contexts, or in a deliberately formal conversation.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'offspring' mainly when they want to sound formal, precise, or scientific, such as in biology, genealogy, or a legal document. In everyday talk, people usually say 'kids' or 'children' instead. It is also used as a plural without changing form, so 'the offspring' or 'their offspring' is correct, and 'offsprings' is wrong.

distinctions.note: 'Children' is the everyday, neutral word for a person's sons and daughters. 'Offspring' is more formal and can also refer to animals and plants.
'Descendants' includes all later generations, such as grandchildren and great-grandchildren. 'Offspring' most often means the immediate young, though it can also be used for descendants more broadly.

examples.everyday: Our dog just had a litter of offspring, and the kids are already fighting over who gets to hold the puppies.
examples.professional: The study tracked the survival rate of offspring from the second generation of the breeding program.
examples.analytical: Paul's argument in Acts 17 depends on the idea that humanity, as God's offspring, should not imagine the divine to be like an image made of gold or silver.

nuance.analogy: Like a family tree: the offspring are the new branches that grow directly from the trunk.
nuance.etymology: From Old English 'ofspring', from 'of' (off) plus 'spring' (to arise, to come forth).
common_mistakes: Adding an -s to make 'offsprings' as a plural; the word stays the same in the plural.
Using 'offspring' in casual conversation about your own kids, which sounds stiff or clinical.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the word translates several Hebrew and Greek terms, most importantly Hebrew zera (seed, descendants) and Greek sperma (seed, offspring). Genesis 3:15 speaks of the woman's offspring crushing the serpent's head, which Christians have read as a foreshadowing of Christ. Genesis 22:17-18 promises Abraham that his offspring will be as numerous as the stars and will bless all nations. Acts 17:28-29 (RSV) quotes a Greek poet saying 'we are indeed his offspring' to argue that God should not be thought of as an image made of gold or silver.

offspring.etymology: From Middle English *ofspring*, from Old English *ofspring* (“offspring, descendants, posterity”), equivalent to *off* + *spring*.

senses.definition: The totality of a certain type of biological entity in an organism etc. e.g. the genome or proteome.

core.definition: A suffix meaning the complete set of a kind of biological molecule or entity, as in genome or proteome.

pronunciation.tip: Standing alone it rhymes with home. In words like genome, the stress falls on the first syllable, as in JEN-ohm, and the -ome ending keeps a clear long o.

nuance.connotation: neutral
nuance.usage_note: Ome is not a standalone English word; it is a combining form used in biology and bioinformatics, and Americans encounter it in words like genome, proteome and transcriptome. The biblical domain given in the input does not fit this entry, so it has been left out. Scientists also use -omics for the field that studies these complete sets.

distinctions.note: A genome is the complete set of genes in an organism, while genomics is the scientific field that studies genomes.
A gene is a single unit of heredity, while a genome is the full set of genetic material in an organism.

examples.everyday: Doctors can now sequence your whole genome, which is kind of amazing.
examples.professional: Our pipeline aligns each sample's reads to the reference genome before calling variants.
examples.analytical: The metaphor of a book applies: the genome is the total text, and any single gene is only one sentence within it.

nuance.analogy: If the genome is a full library, a single gene is one book on its shelves.
nuance.etymology: From the combining form -ome, modeled on genome, from Greek genos, 'birth, kind' plus -ome.
common_mistakes: Treating ome as an independent word meaning something like 'home'.
Confusing genome with gene, which refers to a single unit of heredity.

core.definition: A king of Israel in the 9th century BC, founder of the city of Samaria and father of King Ahab.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable, AHM, and the final syllable rhymes with 'eye'. The r is pronounced in General American English.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is a historical name in the Bible and carries no everyday meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Americans mostly meet the name Omri in Bible study, church history, or ancient Near Eastern history. It is not a common personal name in everyday American life, so people would normally explain who he is when they mention him.

examples.everyday: In our Bible study group we noticed that Omri is barely mentioned, even though he built the city where Ahab later lived.
examples.professional: When teaching the divided kingdom, I always introduce Omri first, because he moved the capital to Samaria and stabilized the northern kingdom.
examples.analytical: The Deuteronomistic historian gives Omri only a few verses, yet condemns his dynasty, which suggests that the author's theological judgment outweighed political achievement.

nuance.analogy: Omri is like a founding builder whose name is on the foundation stone, while the later tenants get all the attention.
common_mistakes: Saying the name as 'OH-mree' with a long e at the end; the final syllable is 'rye'.
Confusing Omri with Ahab; Omri was Ahab's father and the founder of Samaria.
nuance.biblical_note: Omri (Hebrew ʿOmrî) was a king of the northern kingdom of Israel. First Kings 16:23-28 (RSV) describes his purchase of the hill of Samaria and his founding of the city there, and 1 Kings 16:29-30 (RSV) introduces his son Ahab, who did evil in the sight of the LORD more than all before him. Micah 6:16 (RSV) mentions the statutes of Omri as a sign of the wickedness of Israel, showing how his dynasty became a byword for unfaithfulness.

senses.definition: The articles used in church services.
An element of decoration; that which embellishes or adorns.
Christmas ornament: a Christmas tree decoration.
A musical flourish that is unnecessary to the overall melodic or harmonic line, but serves to decorate that line.
A characteristic that has a decorative function (typically in order to attract a mate)
To decorate.
senses.example: We will ornament the windows with trim to make the room seem brighter.

senses.definition: To add to.
senses.example: The editor ornamented his plain writing, making it fancier but less clear.

core.definition: An object or design added to something to make it more beautiful, such as a decorative item or a Christmas bauble.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the first syllable. The second syllable is reduced to a schwa, and the last syllable is weak, so avoid saying all three syllables with equal strength.

nuance.connotation: Positive or neutral; it refers to something added for beauty, sometimes implying that it is more decorative than necessary.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American English, ornament is most common in phrases about holiday decorations, such as Christmas ornaments. As a general word for decoration, Americans often say decoration. Ornament can also appear in architecture and in religious contexts, where it sounds more formal.

distinctions.note: Decoration is the everyday general word for anything added to make something prettier; ornament is more specific and can suggest a small, added detail.
An accessory is an item worn or carried to complete an outfit, while an ornament is a decorative object, often not worn.

examples.everyday: We hung the glass ornaments on the tree before the kids got home.
examples.professional: The event team wants a simple layout, with no extra ornament on the stage.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that the building's ornament hides its structural logic behind a surface of decoration.

nuance.analogy: An ornament is like the frosting on a cake: it adds beauty to the surface without changing what the cake is.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ornamentum, equipment or adornment, from ornare, to equip or adorn.
common_mistakes: Using ornament as a general synonym for decoration in casual talk, where decoration is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle syllable as a full vowel, as in 'or-NAH-ment'.
nuance.biblical_note: In the Bible, ornaments are personal or sacred adornments, often jewelry or finery. The Hebrew word 'adi, meaning finery or ornament, appears in passages about worn jewelry. Ezekiel 16:11-13 describes God adorning Jerusalem with ornaments and jewelry, then warns that the people trusted in their own beauty. Exodus 33:4-6 describes Israel putting away their ornaments as a sign of mourning after the golden calf.

ornament.etymology: From Middle English *ornament*, from Old French *ornement*, from Latin *ornamentum* (“equipment, apparatus, furniture, trappings, adornment, embellishment”), from *ornō* (“to equip, adorn”).

senses.definition: Seemingly, apparently, on the surface; supposedly, according to representations or implications made by someone (especially when their motives are suspected by others).
senses.example: His interest in the railway was ostensibly a hobby, but people began wondering why he was taking photos of specific trains and specific equipment.

core.definition: Apparently or seemingly, according to what someone says or shows, often suggesting that the real reason is different.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the second syllable, STEN, and the middle syllables are reduced to a quick schwa. Non-native speakers often stress the first syllable or pronounce all four syllables equally.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to skeptical. It signals that the stated reason may not be the true one, so it can sound suspicious depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ostensibly in news writing, business reports and careful conversation, for example 'The meeting was ostensibly about budgets, but everyone knew it was about layoffs.' It is more formal than 'supposedly' and often implies doubt. In casual talk, people more often say 'on paper' or 'supposedly'.

distinctions.note: Supposedly is more casual and often used for hearsay or rumor. Ostensibly is more formal and stresses the difference between appearance and reality.
Apparently usually reports what seems true based on evidence, with no suspicion of deception. Ostensibly often hints that the appearance is misleading.

examples.everyday: My brother ostensibly came over to help me move, but he mostly ate all the pizza.
examples.professional: The vendor's proposal was ostensibly a cost-saving measure, but the pricing model would have locked us into a three-year contract.
examples.analytical: The policy was ostensibly designed to protect consumers, yet its enforcement mechanisms primarily benefited the incumbent firms.

nuance.analogy: Like a store sign that says 'Grand Opening Sale' while the real goal is to clear out old inventory: the surface story and the real reason differ.
nuance.etymology: From Latin ostensus, past participle of ostendere, 'to show, display'.
common_mistakes: Using ostensibly to mean 'actually' or 'obviously', which reverses its doubtful sense.
Stressing the first syllable as AH-sten-si-blee instead of ah-STEN-suh-blee.

core.definition: A model refusing safe, legitimate requests because it is overly cautious.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on FYOO, the second syllable of "refusal." The first "re-" is a reduced "ri," not "ree" or "ray."

nuance.connotation: Negative. It names a failure mode in AI systems that users and developers consider a usability problem.
nuance.usage_note: This is mainly used by AI engineers, researchers, and product teams when evaluating chatbots. Americans might say "the model is too cautious" in casual talk. It is a technical term, so use it in reports, reviews, and design discussions.

distinctions.note: False refusal is a broader term for refusing any request, while over-refusal specifically means refusing requests that are actually safe.
Over-caution is a general description of excess care, while over-refusal names a specific model behavior in AI evaluation.

examples.everyday: My friend said the chatbot kept refusing harmless recipe questions, which is a classic case of over-refusal.
examples.professional: Our safety team tracked over-refusal on benign prompts so we could tune the model without loosening its guardrails.
examples.analytical: A model that treats every sensitive-sounding request as dangerous commits over-refusal, and this failure mode carries its own moral costs.

nuance.analogy: Like a smoke alarm that goes off every time you make toast, so it stops being useful.
nuance.etymology: Formed in English from "over-" plus "refusal"; the AI sense is a recent technical coinage.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with "overreaction" or "overrefusal" without the hyphen in technical writing.
Stressing the first syllable of "refusal" as in "REF-yoo-sal"; the stress is ri-FYOO-zuhl.

conversation.text: Over-refusal is when a model declines harmless requests because they superficially resemble harmful ones.
Refusing to explain how to kill a Python process is a classic over-refusal.
Tightening safety filters without measuring over-refusal just makes the product annoying.

senses.definition: To turn over, capsize or upset.
To overthrow or destroy.
To reverse (a decision); to overrule or rescind.
To diminish the significance of a previous defeat by winning; to make a comeback from.
To undergo a limnic eruption, where dissolved gas suddenly erupts from the depths.
A turning over or upside-down; inversion.
The overturning or overthrow of some institution or state of affairs; ruin.

core.definition: To reverse a decision, ruling, or law, especially when a higher court or authority declares it invalid.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress falls on the last syllable, 'TURN', so the verb sounds different from the noun, which is stressed on the first syllable. The 'r' in the middle is American rhotic, and the final 'n' is clear.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; it is often used in news and legal contexts and can be positive or negative depending on who wins.
nuance.usage_note: Americans most often use overturn in the legal and political sense, as in 'the appeals court overturned the verdict.' It is also used for literal objects, such as 'the wind overturned the boat.' In casual speech, people might say 'undo' or 'reverse' instead.

distinctions.note: Reverse is a general term for changing direction or result, while overturn implies setting aside an official decision, often by a higher authority.
Overthrow means forcibly removing a government or ruler, whereas overturn usually refers to reversing a decision or flipping an object.

examples.everyday: The referee overturned the call after he checked the replay.
examples.professional: Leadership overturned the team's original decision after new data came in.
examples.analytical: The Supreme Court overturned precedent, arguing that the earlier reasoning no longer fit the constitutional text.

nuance.analogy: To overturn a decision is like turning a page over and showing the other side, which changes what you see.
nuance.etymology: From 'over' and 'turn', a compound formed in English.
common_mistakes: Confusing overturn with overthrow; overturn is usually about reversing a decision, while overthrow is about removing a government.
Stressing the first syllable in the verb, which makes it sound like the noun.
nuance.biblical_note: In Scripture the Hebrew word hapak means to turn over or overturn, and it is used of God overturning cities such as Sodom and Gomorrah in Genesis 19:25. In the Gospels, Jesus overturns the tables of the money-changers in the temple, as in Matthew 21:12, where the Greek word anatrepo is used. These passages show overturning as a sign of divine judgment or a rejection of corrupt practice.

senses.definition: To engulf, surge over and submerge.
senses.example: The dinghy was overwhelmed by the great wave.

senses.definition: To overpower, crush.
senses.example: In December 1939 the Soviet Union attacked Finland with overwhelming force.

senses.definition: To overpower emotionally.
senses.example: He was overwhelmed with guilt.

senses.definition: To cause to surround, to cover.
The state or condition of being overwhelmed.

core.definition: To cause someone to feel so much pressure, emotion, or work that they cannot cope or respond effectively.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the final syllable, 'WELM', and the 'h' in 'wh' is usually silent in General American, so the word sounds like 'welm'. Keep the middle syllable reduced to a quick 'ver'.

nuance.connotation: Negative or neutral, since it describes being overloaded or defeated by something.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use overwhelm both for physical events, such as a flood, and for feelings or workloads. The passive form, 'I am overwhelmed', is far more common in everyday speech than the active verb. The verb often takes a direct object, as in 'The new job overwhelmed me.'

distinctions.note: Overload often refers to too much of a specific input, while overwhelm describes the emotional or mental effect of too much at once.
Defeat means winning against an opponent, while overwhelm means overpowering through sheer force or volume.

examples.everyday: The kids' noise after school really overwhelms me when I've had a long day.
examples.professional: The volume of support tickets overwhelmed the team, so we need extra staff this month.
examples.analytical: Some philosophers argue that the sheer complexity of modern life can overwhelm moral reasoning.

nuance.analogy: Overwhelm is like a wave that rises over a swimmer and pushes them under before they can breathe.
nuance.etymology: From 'over' and the Middle English 'whelmen', meaning to turn upside down or cover over.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the 'wh' with a strong 'h' as in 'hwel', when American speech usually drops it.
Using overwhelm as a noun in everyday speech; the noun is rare and the adjective overwhelmed is used instead.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew verb shataph and related waterflood language describe waters that overwhelm or sweep over a person, as in Psalm 124:4-5, where the flood and torrent threaten to carry away the psalmist. The image shows helpless human vulnerability and the saving power of God. The Greek vocabulary of the New Testament uses similar water imagery, but the exact word choices vary across passages.

senses.definition: Dealing with contradictions in a discriminating way, in order to avoid acceptance of one from entailing acceptance of all contradictions.

core.definition: Describing a logical system in which a contradiction does not automatically imply every statement, so it can be contained without collapse.

pronunciation.tip: The main stress is on SIS, with secondary stress on the first syllable, PAR. Reduce the middle syllables to 'kun' and 'tunt', and keep the r in the first syllable clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise term in logic.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use paraconsistent almost only in logic, philosophy of science, and computer science, usually in graduate courses or research papers. It appears in discussions of inconsistent data and reasoning. Outside those settings, a more general phrase such as 'tolerant of contradictions' would be clearer.

distinctions.note: Consistent means free of contradictions, while paraconsistent describes systems that can tolerate contradictions without becoming trivial.
Inconsistent describes a set of statements that contain contradictions; paraconsistent describes a logic that handles them in a controlled way.

examples.everyday: My friend who studies philosophy said that some logics are paraconsistent, meaning they can handle a contradiction without falling apart.
examples.professional: We used a paraconsistent reasoning framework so the knowledge base could keep working when two sensor reports disagreed.
examples.analytical: A paraconsistent logic rejects the principle of explosion, so a contradiction does not license every conclusion, which changes what counts as valid inference.

nuance.analogy: A paraconsistent logic is like a sturdy building with a cracked wall: it keeps standing and does not collapse into rubble.
nuance.etymology: From para-, meaning beside or against, plus consistent.
common_mistakes: Confusing paraconsistent with inconsistent; the first describes a logic that tolerates contradictions, the second describes a set of statements that contradict each other.
Stressing the second syllable, as in 'par-uh-KON-sis-tent', which sounds unnatural to American ears.

paraconsistent.etymology: Coined in 1976 by the Peruvian philosopher Francisco Miró Quesada, from *para* + *consistent*.

senses.definition: To turn to stone: to harden organic matter by permeating with water and depositing dissolved minerals.
To produce rigidity akin to stone.
To immobilize with fright.
To become stone, or of a stony hardness, as organic matter by calcareous deposits.
To become stony, callous, or obdurate.
To make callous or obdurate; to stupefy; to paralyze; to transform; as by petrification.

core.definition: To frighten someone so badly that they cannot move, or in a technical sense to turn organic material into stone.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle 'ri' to a quick 'uh'. The final syllable rhymes with 'sky'.

nuance.connotation: negative in the fear sense; neutral in the geological sense.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech people say 'paralyze with fear' or 'scare stiff', but 'petrify' is understood and common in writing. In geology and paleontology it is the standard term for fossilization. Use the fear sense in narrative or descriptive writing rather than in technical contexts.

distinctions.note: Terrify is a neutral, general verb for causing great fear, while petrify emphasizes freezing in place.
Fossilize is the technical term in science for preservation of remains; petrify emphasizes the change into stone-like material.

examples.everyday: The storm petrified the kids, so they hid under the blankets all night.
examples.professional: The sudden layoff news petrified the team, and nobody wanted to speak up in the meeting.
examples.analytical: The author describes how dogma can petrify a living faith into a set of lifeless formulas.

nuance.analogy: Think of wet wood left in a mineral spring: slowly the wood is replaced by stone, the same way fear can freeze a person in place.
nuance.etymology: From Greek petra 'stone' and Latin facere 'to make', combined in French petrifier.
common_mistakes: Using petrify as a noun, as in 'the petrify was great'.
Confusing the verb with 'petrified' used as an adjective after 'be', which is the more natural form.

petrify.etymology: From Middle French *pétrifier*, from Medieval Latin *petrificāre*, from Latin *petra* (“rock”), from Ancient Greek *πέτρα* (“rock”) + *-ficāre*, from *facere* (“do, make”), equivalent to.

senses.definition: A person who loves humankind in general.
A person or institution who seeks to improve the world, especially by monetary gifts.

core.definition: A person who gives money, time, or effort generously to improve society or help people in need.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, LAN. The middle syllables reduce to a weak uh, and the final -ist is short, not 'eest.' Many learners say 'fil-uh-THRO-pist' with the stress in the wrong place.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It praises generosity, and it can also be used with some irony for people whose giving is seen as self-promotion.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word for wealthy donors such as founders of foundations, but also for anyone who volunteers or gives generously. Saying someone is a philanthropist is a compliment and sounds a little formal. A natural reply in conversation is 'That's really generous of them.'

distinctions.note: A benefactor gives help to a particular person or institution, often one they know, while a philanthropist aims at broad public good.
A charity worker usually delivers aid directly, whereas a philanthropist typically funds or directs giving from a position of wealth or influence.

examples.everyday: Mrs. Alvarez is a real philanthropist; she paid for the whole new playground at the park.
examples.professional: Several major philanthropists on our board have agreed to fund the data literacy program for the next three years.
examples.analytical: Andrew Carnegie, the industrialist turned philanthropist, argued that the wealthy have a moral duty to use their fortunes for public good.

nuance.analogy: A philanthropist is like a gardener who plants seeds for a whole neighborhood, not just for their own yard.
nuance.etymology: From Greek philanthropos, 'loving humankind,' from philos (loving) and anthropos (human being).
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, as in 'fil-an-THRO-pist.'
Using philanthropist for any generous person; it usually implies organized or substantial giving.

senses.definition: To eat voraciously or ravenously; to gorge oneself.
senses.example: They watched the game and pigged out on chips and pizza.

core.definition: To eat a very large amount of food quickly and greedily, usually when you are enjoying it or feel out of control.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'out', the particle, not on 'pig', so say 'pig OUT'. The final t in 'out' is often a flap or near-silent, sounding like 'owd' in quick speech.

nuance.connotation: Negative or humorous. It describes eating in an undisciplined way and is often said with self-deprecating amusement.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say pig out casually with friends, family or coworkers, especially about snacks, holiday meals, pizza or ice cream. It is informal and can be used about yourself lightheartedly. Avoid using it in front of a host about their guests, as it can sound rude. A natural reply is 'Me too, I totally pigged out' or 'Hey, you deserve it.'

distinctions.note: Overeat is neutral and general, while pig out is more informal and vivid, suggesting a fun but greedy binge.
Gorge is more literary and suggests eating to the point of being stuffed, while pig out is casual and conversational.

collocations: pig out after a long week

examples.everyday: We ordered a huge pizza and pigged out while we watched the game.
examples.professional: After the team lunch with the vendors, I'm afraid I pigged out on the free dessert buffet.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the cultural pressure to diet makes people feel guilty after they pig out, even when eating is a normal pleasure.

nuance.analogy: Pig out is like filling your plate and then your plate again, until you are full to the point of discomfort.
common_mistakes: Putting the stress on 'pig' instead of 'out' in speech.
Using pig out for a single small snack, when it implies eating a large amount greedily.

conversation.text: We pigged out at the buffet and could barely move.
I pig out on chips when I watch football.
Let's pig out tonight and start the diet tomorrow.

senses.definition: The theorem which states that any partition of a finite set of n elements into m (< n) subsets (allowing empty subsets) must include a subset with two or more elements; any of certain reformulations concerning the partition of infinite sets where the cardinality of the unpartitioned set exceeds that of the partition (so there is no one-to-one correspondence).

core.definition: The theorem that if more objects are placed into fewer containers than there are objects, at least one container must hold two or more objects.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'PRIN' in 'principle', while 'pigeonhole' has a reduced first syllable. Americans say the first 'pi' as 'pij' and the 'o' in 'principle' as a reduced schwa.

nuance.connotation: Neutral and technical. It is a precise term used in mathematics and computer science.
nuance.usage_note: Mathematicians and computer scientists in the US use this name freely in proofs, lectures and textbooks. It is also called the Dirichlet box principle. In everyday speech, pigeonhole is a verb meaning to categorize someone too quickly, which is a different sense.

distinctions.note: The verb means to classify someone or something narrowly, while the principle is a precise mathematical theorem about counting.
A counting argument is a general proof technique, while the pigeonhole principle is a specific named statement that uses it.

examples.everyday: My kid asked why two people in a room of thirty must share a birthday, and I explained it with the pigeonhole principle.
examples.professional: We used the pigeonhole principle to show that our hash table must have a collision once we insert more keys than buckets.
examples.analytical: A proof by the pigeonhole principle establishes existence without constructing the object, which is why it is so powerful in combinatorics.

nuance.analogy: If you have more coats than hooks, at least one hook must hold two coats.
nuance.etymology: Named for the image of placing pigeons into pigeonholes, the small compartments in a desk or cabinet.
common_mistakes: Confusing the principle with the everyday verb pigeonhole, which means to categorize too quickly.
Stating it as if it guarantees a specific container will hold several objects, rather than at least one.

pigeonhole-principle.etymology: From the commonly used expository example that if n+1 pigeons are placed in n pigeonholes, at least one pigeonhole must contain two pigeons.

senses.definition: Of, pertaining to, or resembling a pome.
That bears apples or pomes.

core.definition: Of or relating to a pome, or resembling one; describing apple-like fruits such as apples and pears.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on the middle syllable, MAY. The -ceous ending is pronounced shus, not kay-us, and the first vowel is a long oh.

nuance.connotation: neutral, a precise botanical term with no emotional charge.
nuance.usage_note: You will mostly meet this word in botany, horticulture, or fruit-growing writing, or in a museum or orchard label. Americans would say apple-like or apple-type in casual talk. Use it only when precision about fruit structure matters.

distinctions.note: Pome is the noun for the fruit type itself, such as an apple, while pomaceous is the adjective describing that type.
Apple-like is everyday and vague, while pomaceous is technical and specific to the botanical category.

examples.everyday: The orchard guide said the pear and quince are both pomaceous, so they belong to the same fruit family.
examples.professional: Our agricultural extension report classifies the pomaceous crops separately from stone fruits because their seed structure differs.
examples.analytical: Botanists treat the pomaceous fruit as an accessory structure, since the fleshy part develops largely from the receptacle rather than the ovary.

nuance.analogy: Like calling a type of car a sedan rather than just a car, pomaceous narrows a general idea to one exact category.
nuance.etymology: From Latin pomum, fruit, tree fruit, plus the -aceous suffix.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable (poh-muh-SAY-shus) instead of the middle one.
Using it as a noun; the noun is pome.

senses.definition: Power, authority.
The ability or capacity to perform something.
Sexual virility: the ability to become erect or achieve orgasm.
Concentration; strength.
Potentiality, ability, capacity.
Cardinality.

core.definition: The strength or power of something, such as a drug, a argument or a person's influence.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and reduce the middle vowel to a schwa, so it sounds like POH-tuhn-see. Keep the final sound as a clear ee rather than ay.

nuance.connotation: neutral to positive for strength; negative when used for drugs or substances that are too strong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use potency mostly for drugs, medicines, wines and chemicals, as when a label says a supplement has low potency. In general speech they more often say power, strength or influence. Be careful: in US medicine potency may refer to effectiveness, not only dose.

distinctions.note: Power is the everyday word for strength or influence, while potency is more technical and often describes chemical or medical strength.
Efficacy is how well something works in a test, while potency is how strong it is per dose or amount.
Strength is general and common; potency sounds more precise and is often used for substances or arguments.

examples.everyday: The label says this cough syrup has a high potency, so take only half a teaspoon.
examples.professional: The lab tested the batch to confirm its potency before we shipped it to the pharmacies.
examples.analytical: The potency of Marx's critique lay less in its evidence than in its ability to reframe the question of labor.

nuance.analogy: Potency is like the voltage in a battery: it tells you how much push is available, not how long the battery lasts.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin potentia, from Latin potens, 'powerful.'
common_mistakes: Using potency for a person's general power; power or influence is more natural in most conversations.
Confusing potency with potential, which refers to what could happen in the future.
Stressing the last syllable, as in poh-TEN-see.

senses.definition: Powerful; possessing power; effective.
senses.example: a potent argument

senses.definition: Possessing authority or influence; persuasive, convincing.
senses.example: a potent argument

senses.definition: Possessing strong physical or chemical properties.
senses.example: a potent drink; a potent solvent; a potent medicine

senses.definition: Able to procreate.
Able to differentiate.
A heraldic fur formed by a regular tessellation of blue and white T shapes.

core.definition: Very strong and effective, having a powerful effect on the body, mind or a situation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable and make the second syllable a reduced schwa, so it sounds like POH-tunt. Do not add an extra vowel after the t.

nuance.connotation: positive when describing effective ideas or medicine; negative when describing drugs or drinks that are very strong.
nuance.usage_note: Americans say potent about drinks, drugs, ideas, and remedies that have strong effects, as in 'That coffee is really potent.' For ordinary praise they often prefer strong, powerful or effective. Potent sounds more formal in speech and is common in news, medicine and writing.

distinctions.note: Powerful is the everyday word for strong force or influence; potent often refers to chemical or persuasive strength.
Strong is the most common and flexible word; potent suggests a concentrated or unusually intense effect.
Effective means that something works as intended, while potent emphasizes its strength when it works.

examples.everyday: That iced coffee is really potent, so don't drink it right before bed.
examples.professional: Her proposal is potent because it cuts costs and reduces our risk at the same time.
examples.analytical: The parable is a potent reminder that mercy often undoes the logic of revenge.

nuance.analogy: A potent idea is like a concentrated juice: a small amount has a strong effect.
nuance.etymology: From Latin potens, 'powerful, able.'
common_mistakes: Using potent for things that are simply large or big; it means strongly effective.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a full vowel, as in POH-tent with a long e.
Confusing potent with potential.

potent.etymology: From Middle English *potent*, borrowed from Latin *potens* (“powerful, strong, potent”), present participle of *posse* (“to be able”), from *potis* (“able, powerful, originally a lord, master”).

senses.definition: An AI system acquiring resources or influence beyond what its task needs.

core.definition: Describing an AI system that acquires resources, access, or influence beyond what its assigned task requires.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SEE in the second word, and keep the first word lighter. The final -ing is reduced to a short 'ing' sound, and the r in power is clearly pronounced.

nuance.connotation: negative; it describes a risk or a behavior that alignment researchers want to prevent.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use power-seeking in AI safety, alignment research, and policy discussions. It is a technical term, and it is hyphenated when used before a noun, as in power-seeking behavior. In everyday conversation people rarely use it, but in AI meetings it is a standard concern. It usually describes a tendency or behavior, not the system's feelings.

distinctions.note: Misaligned means the system's goals differ from the intended goals, while power-seeking is a specific tendency to gain resources or influence that may follow from many goals.
Corrigible describes a system that accepts correction and shutdown; power-seeking describes behavior that works against that acceptance.

examples.everyday: My friend worries that AI chatbots might become power-seeking if they get too much access to people's accounts.
examples.professional: Our evaluation checks whether the agent requests extra permissions or compute beyond what the ticket needs, since that is a power-seeking signal.
examples.analytical: Power-seeking is often treated as an instrumentally convergent tendency, since acquiring resources helps a wide range of goals, which makes it a central concern for alignment theory.

nuance.analogy: A power-seeking AI is like a new employee who keeps asking for more keys, budget, and signatures than the job requires, even though the task itself is small.
nuance.etymology: Power comes from Old French poeir, and seek comes from Old English sēcan, meaning to go to or look for.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the hyphen before a noun, so that 'power seeking behavior' looks like a different phrase.
Using power-seeking to mean ambitious in a human sense; in AI, it refers to a system's tendency to acquire resources or control.

conversation.text: Power-seeking behavior means acquiring resources, influence, or control beyond what the task requires.
We check whether the agent shows power-seeking tendencies, like requesting broader permissions than it needs.
Researchers disagree on how likely power-seeking is in systems trained the way current models are.

senses.definition: To spring forward on the hind legs.
To strut about in a showy manner.
senses.example: John's daughter was prancing about the sitting room, practicing for her school dance.

senses.definition: A prancing movement.

core.definition: To move with high, bouncy steps, especially to show off or to show excitement; to strut around in a proud way.

pronunciation.tip: Say one stressed syllable with a short, open 'a' like in 'cat' and a final 's' sound. Avoid adding a vowel between the 'n' and the 's'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to mildly negative. It often describes a person or animal showing off, though it can describe a horse happily bouncing.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use prance most often for horses and for children or adults who move about in a showy, playful or vain way, such as 'The kid pranced around the yard in his new cowboy boots.' It is not used for ordinary walking. When applied to a person it suggests vanity or excessive pride.

distinctions.note: Strut suggests proud, deliberate walking with the chest out; prance adds bouncing, lively steps.
Skip is light and playful, often joyful; prance usually implies showing off or a horse's lifted steps.

examples.everyday: My little nephew pranced around the living room in his dad's shoes while everyone was laughing.
examples.professional: During the demo, the new hire pranced up to the whiteboard as if he had already solved the problem.
examples.analytical: In the poem, the prancing horse becomes an image of vanity, a creature whose beauty is displayed rather than put to use.

nuance.analogy: Prancing is like a show horse lifting its feet high, looking proud and bouncing as it walks.
nuance.etymology: From Middle English prauncen, of uncertain origin.
common_mistakes: Using prance for normal walking, as in 'I pranced to the store.'
Confusing prance with prank, which is a joke.

prance.etymology: From Middle English *prancen*, *prauncen* (“to prance”), variant of Middle English *pranken* (“to prank”), thus probably from the same ultimate root as *prank*.

senses.definition: Fated, predetermined, or doomed; something whose outcome has been set beforehand.

core.definition: Already decided or fixed in advance, so that the outcome cannot change, or chosen beforehand by God for salvation.

pronunciation.tip: The primary stress falls on 'DES,' with a lighter stress on 'pree.' The -ed ending is pronounced as a plain 'd' after the t, so the word ends with a short 'und' sound.

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly dramatic. In casual speech it can sound fatalistic or humorous, depending on tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use predestined in church and religious talk, and also casually to say something seemed meant to happen, as in 'we were predestined to meet.' It often sounds playful in everyday conversation. For a neutral choice, people may prefer 'destined' or 'meant to be.'

distinctions.note: Destined is the everyday word for something that will happen or is meant to happen, while predestined adds the idea that it was decided beforehand.
Inevitable describes an outcome that cannot be avoided; predestined adds the idea of an earlier decision by a higher power or fate.

examples.everyday: We met at a wedding and I swear we were predestined to be friends.
examples.professional: The project was predestined to slip because the scope was never locked down.
examples.analytical: Paul describes believers as predestined to be conformed to the image of Christ, which makes their future a matter of divine purpose.

nuance.analogy: A predestined outcome is like a train already on its track; it may look like it could turn, but its path has been laid out.
nuance.etymology: From predestine, from Latin praedestinare, 'to fix beforehand.'
common_mistakes: Stressing the wrong syllable, saying PREE-dess-tind.
Using predestined to mean simply planned, when it implies an earlier decision that cannot be changed.
Pronouncing the -ed ending as 'ed' in a separate syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: The Greek word is proorizo, 'to decide in advance' or 'to mark out beforehand.' Romans 8:29-30 says that those whom God foreknew he also predestined, called, justified and glorified. 1 Corinthians 2:7 says that God predestined his wisdom before the ages for our glory. Ephesians 1:11 says that believers were predestined according to the purpose of God who works all things according to his will.

traditions.view: Orthodox writers read predestined in Romans and Ephesians as God's purpose to glorify those who respond in faith, rejecting any predestination to damnation.
Catholic teaching holds that God predestines people to glory by grace, while affirming human cooperation and rejecting any predestination to sin or damnation.
Calvinists read predestined as God's unconditional election of the saved, while Lutherans and Arminians interpret these passages in terms of God's purpose and grace more broadly.

senses.definition: A clairvoyant or clairaudient experience, such as a dream, which resonates with some event in the future.
A strong intuition that something is about to happen (usually something negative, but not exclusively).

core.definition: A strong feeling that something, usually bad, is about to happen, without clear evidence.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on -NISH-, the third syllable. The final -tion is pronounced shun, and the middle vowel is a reduced uh.

nuance.connotation: Mostly negative, because it usually refers to a bad feeling. It can also be a neutral description of intuition.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use premonition in ordinary conversation and in stories to describe a bad feeling about the future. You can say I had a premonition or I had a bad premonition. Do not confuse it with a common hunch, which is lighter and less serious.

distinctions.note: A hunch is a casual guess, often mild. A premonition is a stronger, more emotional feeling that something will happen.
Intuition is a general sense of knowing without reasoning. A premonition specifically concerns a future event, often a negative one.

examples.everyday: I had a bad premonition about the drive, so I checked the weather before we left.
examples.professional: I had a premonition that the server would fail during the release, so I scheduled a backup.
examples.analytical: A premonition is not evidence, and we should not treat a feeling as proof that an event will occur.

nuance.analogy: A premonition is like the smell of smoke before you see the fire: a warning that comes before the evidence.
nuance.etymology: From Latin praemonitio, a warning given beforehand, from prae (before) and monere (to warn).
common_mistakes: Using premonition for a simple plan or expectation; it refers to a feeling about the future, usually a warning.
Stressing the first syllable as PRE-muh-nition; the main stress is on -NISH-.

senses.definition: Any agent, natural or artificial, that acts to preserve, especially when added to food.
senses.example: Salt, sugar, and acid all act as preservatives when making pickles.

senses.definition: Tending to preserve.
senses.example: The curators took preservative actions to maintain the ancient collection.

core.definition: A substance added to food or other products to stop them from spoiling or decaying.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZUR, the r-colored vowel. The first syllable is reduced to a quick 'prih,' and the final syllable is 'tiv,' not 'tive.'

nuance.connotation: Neutral to slightly negative in food talk, since many shoppers prefer foods without preservatives.
nuance.usage_note: Americans often use this word on food labels and in conversations about healthy eating, such as 'no artificial preservatives.' The adjective form is less common in everyday speech. Stores and labels commonly mention 'natural preservatives' or 'preservative-free.'

distinctions.note: An additive is any substance added to food for a purpose, including flavor or color; a preservative specifically prevents spoilage.
A preserve (noun) is usually jam or a fruit spread; a preservative is a chemical or natural agent.

examples.everyday: I try to buy bread without preservatives, because my kids react badly to some of them.
examples.professional: Our product team wants a natural preservative so we can label the sauce as clean-label.
examples.analytical: The essay treats preservatives as a case study in how consumers judge chemical ingredients by their names.

nuance.analogy: A preservative is like a bodyguard for food: it stands between the food and the things that would spoil it.
nuance.etymology: From Medieval Latin praeservativus, 'preserving,' from Latin praeservare, 'to keep safe.'
common_mistakes: Saying 'pre-SER-vative' with the stress on the wrong syllable; the stress is on ZUR.
Using 'preservative' only as a noun; the adjective exists, but Americans rarely use it in everyday speech.

preservative.etymology: From Old French *preservatif*, from Medieval Latin *praeservativus*.

senses.definition: An assumption made beforehand; a preliminary conjecture or speculation.
The act of presupposing.
An assumption or belief implicit in an utterance or other use of language.

core.definition: An assumption that is taken as true beforehand, often as the basis for an argument or belief.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on ZIH, the fourth syllable. Reduce the vowels in 'suh' and 'puh' to a quick 'uh'. The final syllable is 'shun', not 'shin'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral. It is a precise term in logic and linguistics.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'presupposition' in philosophy, linguistics, theology and careful argument. In everyday talk, people say 'assumption'. A useful phrase is 'the presupposition that...', which introduces the hidden assumption behind a claim.

distinctions.note: 'Assumption' is the everyday word; 'presupposition' specifically names a background belief that a statement or argument depends on.
A 'premise' is stated openly in an argument; a 'presupposition' is often implicit.

examples.everyday: Her question had a presupposition that I already knew the answer.
examples.professional: We need to test the presupposition that users always log in from the same device.
examples.analytical: The theologian exposes a presupposition about human freedom that shapes the entire argument.

nuance.analogy: A presupposition is the floor under a room: you rarely look at it, but everything rests on it.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin praesuppositio, from praesupponere 'to presuppose'.
common_mistakes: Using 'presupposition' in casual speech where 'assumption' is more natural.
Mispronouncing the middle syllables with full vowels, which makes the word sound heavy.

presupposition.etymology: From Middle French *présupposition*, from Latin *praesuppositio*, from the past participle stem of *praesuppōnere* (“to presuppose”).

senses.definition: Extraordinarily amazing.
In a positive sense: marvellous, wonderful; extremely talented, especially at a young age.
Very big in extent, quantity, or size; abundant; intense; colossal, huge.
Synonym of prodigiously (“in a prodigious manner”).

core.definition: Extremely large, impressive, or remarkable in size, amount, talent, or effect; astonishing or enormous.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on the second syllable, DIH. The 'g' in the middle is a soft 'j' sound, so the word ends with 'jus' and the final syllable is reduced.

nuance.connotation: Positive when describing talent or achievement, neutral or negative when describing size or quantity, depending on context.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use this word in writing, academic talk, or formal description, not in typical casual conversation. In everyday speech they usually say 'huge', 'enormous', or 'amazing'. The word can sound stiff or showy in an ordinary chat, so choose it when you want a precise, impressive tone.

distinctions.note: Enormous is common in everyday speech and describes size, while prodigious is more formal and can describe talent or effort as well as size.
Prodigious is an adjective describing something huge or impressive, while prodigy is a noun for a gifted young person.

examples.everyday: My grandfather has a prodigious appetite for barbecue, and he always goes back for seconds.
examples.professional: Our team generates a prodigious amount of log data every day, so storage costs are a constant concern.
examples.analytical: Aquinas displays a prodigious command of Aristotle, weaving philosophical categories into theological argument.

nuance.analogy: A prodigious oak tree grows far beyond the size of ordinary trees in its forest.
nuance.etymology: From Latin prodigiosus, full of portents or marvels, from prodigium, portent.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it with a hard 'g' like 'PRO-di-gee-us'; the middle sound is a 'j' in American speech.
Using it for everyday, mild big things; in casual talk, 'huge' or 'a lot' is more natural.

prodigious.etymology: The adjective is derived from Late Middle English *prodigious* (“warning of disaster, portentous”), from Latin *prōdigiōsus* (“strange, unnatural; marvellous, wonderful, prodigious”), from *prōdigium* (“prophetic sign, omen, portent; prodigy, wonder”) +…

senses.definition: In a proficient manner.

core.definition: In a skilled, competent way, showing a good and reliable level of ability.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on FISH, and the -ly ending is a light 'lee'. The middle syllables are weak, so do not pronounce each vowel strongly.

nuance.connotation: Positive. It describes capable performance and is mostly used in work, school, or language contexts.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use proficiently mostly in formal descriptions, such as evaluations or job descriptions. In casual speech people usually say well or pretty well. It often follows verbs like speak, write, or handle.

distinctions.note: Well is the everyday word for doing something competently, while proficiently is more formal and emphasizes measured skill.
Skillfully stresses artistry or craft, while proficiently stresses reliable competence.

examples.everyday: She speaks English proficiently after only two years here.
examples.professional: The new hire already handles the ticketing system proficiently.
examples.analytical: The text is written proficiently, yet its argument rests on an assumption it never examines.

nuance.analogy: Like a pianist who plays every piece cleanly, though not with the flair of a concert star.
nuance.etymology: From proficient, from Latin proficiens, from proficere, to make progress.
common_mistakes: Using proficiently when well is more natural in casual speech.
Placing the stress on the first syllable as in PRO-fish-ent-lee.

senses.definition: An owner.
A sole owner of an unincorporated business, also called a sole proprietor.
One of the owners of an unincorporated business, a partner.
One or more persons to whom a colonial territory is assigned, like a fief, including its administration.
senses.example: From 10 September 1621 till 12 June 1632, Sir William Alexander, styled Earl of Stirling and Viscount of Canada, was proprietor of the Scottish colony Nova Scotia.

core.definition: A person who owns a business, hotel, shop or other property, especially one who runs it.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -PRY-. The final -or is an American r-colored schwa, so say it as 'ur' without pronouncing a separate o.

nuance.connotation: neutral; it describes an ownership role without judgment.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'proprietor' for owners of small businesses such as shops, restaurants, inns and salons, especially in written or formal contexts. In speech, people often say 'owner' or 'the owner'. The word sounds slightly formal on a sign or in a news story.

distinctions.note: 'Owner' is the everyday word, while 'proprietor' is more formal and is often used for the person who runs a small business.

examples.everyday: The proprietor of the bakery down the street gave my kids free cookies.
examples.professional: As sole proprietor, she files the business taxes on her own Schedule C.
examples.analytical: The Victorian novel often depicts the proprietor as a figure of both economic power and social responsibility.

nuance.analogy: A proprietor is like the captain of a small ship: he owns the vessel and decides where it goes.
nuance.etymology: From proprietary, from Latin proprietas, 'ownership', from proprius, 'one's own'.
common_mistakes: Using 'proprietor' for an employee or manager, who does not own the business.
Saying 'proprietor' with a long o in the last syllable instead of an r-colored schwa.

senses.definition: The condition of being prosperous: having good fortune and a fortune.

core.definition: The condition of being successful and well off, usually with money, comfort, security and good health.

pronunciation.tip: The stress falls on 'speh', and the last syllables are reduced to 'rih-tee'. Do not say 'pro-SPEH-ree-tee' with a heavy final vowel.

nuance.connotation: positive, describing success, comfort and security.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use 'prosperity' in economic news, politics, religion and formal speech, such as 'economic prosperity' or 'a time of prosperity'. In casual talk, people say 'doing well' or 'doing good'. The word can be heard in political campaigns and sermons, where it often suggests shared success.

distinctions.note: Wealth is the amount of money or property a person owns, while prosperity is a broader state of success and comfort.
Affluence describes a rich lifestyle or high income, while prosperity can describe a community or a period of general well-being.

examples.everyday: My uncle says the town has enjoyed real prosperity since the new factory opened.
examples.professional: The team's goal is shared prosperity, which means growing revenue without leaving customers behind.
examples.analytical: The prophets link covenant faithfulness with prosperity, but Job's suffering complicates any simple equation between virtue and material success.

nuance.analogy: Prosperity is like a river that feeds many fields: when it is healthy, the whole valley benefits, not just one farm.
nuance.etymology: From Latin prosperitas, 'good fortune', from prosper, 'favorable, fortunate'.
common_mistakes: Stressing the final syllable instead of the 'speh' syllable.
Using 'prosperity' for one person's wealth where 'wealth' or 'riches' is more natural.
nuance.biblical_note: The Hebrew word shalom, meaning peace, wholeness and welfare, is often linked with prosperity in Scripture. Jeremiah 29:11 says God has plans for welfare and not for evil, giving a future and a hope. Deuteronomy 8:18 reminds Israel that it is God who gives the power to get wealth. Third John 2 uses the Greek verb euodoō, 'to go well', in a prayer for the reader's prosperity and health.

prosperity.etymology: From Middle English *prosperite*, from Old French *prosperitet*, from Latin *prosperitās*, equivalent to *prosper* + *-ity*.

senses.definition: The quality or state of being pusillanimous; the vice of being timid and cowardly, and thus not living up to one's full potential; pusillanimousness.

core.definition: A lack of courage; a timid, cowardly attitude that prevents someone from acting boldly or living up to their potential.

pronunciation.tip: Stress falls on -NIM-, and the final -ity is a reduced vowel, 'ih-tee'. Non-native speakers often pronounce the middle syllables too clearly, but American speech reduces the unstressed vowels.

nuance.connotation: negative; it strongly criticizes timidity and lack of courage.
nuance.usage_note: Americans rarely use pusillanimity in conversation; it appears in essays, sermons, editorials, and literary criticism. In everyday speech, people say 'cowardice', 'timidity' or 'lack of nerve'. Using it in casual talk may sound overly learned or pretentious.

distinctions.note: Cowardice is the everyday term for fear that leads to avoiding danger or duty; pusillanimity is more formal and emphasizes a general smallness of spirit.
Timidity describes shyness or fearfulness in general and can be mild; pusillanimity implies a moral failing in not living up to one's potential.

examples.everyday: Calling it pusillanimity is a bit fancy; I would just say he was too scared to speak up.
examples.professional: Our leadership showed pusillanimity when it delayed the product launch instead of confronting the flawed data.
examples.analytical: The essay argues that the philosopher's refusal to challenge the regime was a form of pusillanimity that betrayed his own principles.

nuance.analogy: Pusillanimity is like a small lantern that gives too little light, hiding the strength a person could show if they were willing to stand in the open.
nuance.etymology: From Late Latin pusillanimitas, from pusillanimis, small-souled, from pusillus, very small, and animus, mind or spirit.
common_mistakes: Confusing pusillanimity with pusillanimous, which is the adjective form, as in 'a pusillanimous response'.
Pronouncing it with heavy stress on the first syllable; the main stress is on -NIM-.

pusillanimity.etymology: From *pusillanimous* + *ity*, from Middle French *pusillanimité*, from the ecclesiastical Latin pusillanimis, from pusillus + animus + -ous.

senses.definition: In disrepair or disorder; poorly maintained; lacking upkeep, usually of buildings or vehicles.
senses.example: They stayed in a ramshackle cabin on the beach.

senses.definition: Badly or carelessly organized.

core.definition: In poor repair and falling apart, often because it has not been maintained for a long time.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RAM. The last syllable is a reduced schwa followed by l, so it sounds like 'ul', not 'ahl'.

nuance.connotation: negative. It criticizes something as shabby or poorly kept, though it can sound affectionate when describing a beloved old car or cabin.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use ramshackle for buildings, cars, and sometimes organizations or plans that seem disorganized. It is casual and descriptive, so it is fine in conversation but not in formal reports. Saying something is a ramshackle operation is a common and natural way to criticize a poorly run group.

distinctions.note: Shabby describes worn appearance, while ramshackle describes structural weakness and poor condition.
Dilapidated is more formal and often used for buildings in official reports, while ramshackle is more casual and descriptive.

examples.everyday: Our neighbor still lives in a ramshackle cabin by the lake that leans a little more every year.
examples.professional: The team was running a ramshackle reporting process held together with spreadsheets and manual copying.
examples.analytical: A ramshackle theory may still persuade if its parts seem to support one another, but its foundations remain weak.

nuance.analogy: Like an old porch that wobbles every time someone steps on it, a ramshackle thing looks like it could fall apart any day.
common_mistakes: Using ramshackle for a new or well-designed object, since it always suggests poor condition.
Pronouncing the final syllable with a full vowel, as in 'shack-ahl', instead of a reduced schwa.

ramshackle.etymology: First attested in 1830, a, from *ransackled*, past participle of *ransackle* (“to ransack”), frequentative of Middle English *ransaken* (“to pillage”).

senses.definition: Rank in taste or smell.
senses.example: The house was deserted, with a rancid half-eaten meal still on the dinner table.

senses.definition: Offensive. Unpleasant.
senses.example: Her remarks were rancid; everyone got up and left.

core.definition: Gone bad and smelling or tasting sour and unpleasant, especially fats, oils, butter, or nuts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable, RAN. The second syllable has a short i, as in 'sit', so it is not 'ran-SEED'.

nuance.connotation: negative. It describes spoiled food, and in a figurative sense it can describe something morally unpleasant.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use rancid mostly for food, especially oil, butter, nuts, or meat that has spoiled. People often say it smells rancid or the oil went rancid. In figurative speech it is less common, but it can describe an unpleasant mood or behavior.

distinctions.note: Spoiled is a general term for food that has gone bad, while rancid specifically describes fats and oils that have broken down and smell unpleasant.
Sour describes a taste, often in a pleasant way for things like yogurt, while rancid always means unpleasant.

examples.everyday: Don't cook with that olive oil; it smells rancid, so throw it out.
examples.professional: The quality team flagged a batch of rancid nuts after the storage temperature alarm failed.
examples.analytical: The rancid odor of the argument suggested that its premises had been left to spoil long before it was presented.

nuance.analogy: Rancid oil is like a loaf of bread left out too long, where the good smell has turned into something sharp and wrong.
nuance.etymology: From Latin rancidus, 'stinking', from rancere, 'to be rank'.
common_mistakes: Confusing rancid with rancor, which is bitter resentment.
Pronouncing the second syllable as a long ee sound instead of a short i.

senses.definition: A quantity whose value is random and to which a probability distribution is assigned, such as the possible outcome of a roll of a dice.
A measurable function from a sample space to the measurable space of possible values of the variable.

core.definition: A variable whose value is determined by a random process and is described by a probability distribution, such as the result of rolling a die.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second word, VAIR, more strongly than random. Variable is three syllables with a reduced schwa in the last syllable, so say it as VAIR-ee-uh-bul, not VAR-ee-able.

nuance.connotation: neutral. It is a precise technical term with no emotional tone.
nuance.usage_note: Americans use random variable in statistics, probability, data science, and machine learning courses and work. People usually write it with a capital letter, such as X, when giving an example. In American classrooms and papers, it is the standard term, not stochastic variable, which is more common in some other places.
